stories.headline: Senator McKelvey explains the legacy of Prince Kūhiō
stories.summary: In his legislative update, Senator Angus McKelvey describes Prince Kūhiō's advocacy for Native Hawaiian rights and the work still left to do.
stories.text: What's the deal with Prince Kohiʻo? Aloha everybody, I'm Senator Angus McKelvey representing West and South Maui and this week we celebrated Prince Kohiʻo Day. Prince Jonah Kohiʻo Kalanaonouli was a prominent figure in Hawaiian history. He was known for his leadership and steadfast advocacy for Native Hawaiian rights. Born on March 26, 1871 into the royal family of He was educated at the Royal School and Punahou School, later studying abroad in California and England. His political career started as a delegate to the U.S. Congress, which he was elected to first in 1902 and held it for nearly two decades. And during that time, he advocated tirelessly for Native Hawaiian rights, including the preservation of Hawaiian land and culture. This led up to the instrumentality of the passage of the Hawaii Homes Commission Act of 1920, which aimed to provide homesteads for Native Hawaiians, founded the Hawaiian Civic Club Movement, and promoted civic engagement and cultural preservation, which was on display yesterday at the Capitol as hundreds came from around Hawaii to celebrate Prince Kohiʻo Day, and remind us of our never-ending duty to the Native Hawaiian people, especially those who are sitting and languishing on the waiting list. Justice denied is justice delayed, and therefore Prince Kohiʻo Day serves as a memory of our never-ending, unfinished work to give back to the Hawaiian people what was lost to them. Aloha and have a great week.

Civil Beat reports that the proof is contained in secret FBI recordings by disgraced Hawaiʻi rep Ty Cullen as part of a federal corruption investigation. The sting also caught Maui representative Kalani English with his hand in the cookie jar. Cullen and English both took bribes from businessman and wastewater magnate Milton Choy. stories.headline: Maui Travels revisits Jay April's 2017 Yosemite trip
stories.summary: Jay April shares a March 2017 visit to Yosemite, with uncrowded trails, snowmelt waterfalls, Half Dome, El Capitan and the Awahnee hotel.
stories.text: My whole life, it's been a dream of mine to go to Yosemite Valley, but I could never get there. It was always too crowded or too far away. But in March of 2017, I found myself in Fresno, 122 miles away, and I said, I'm going. People said, no, there's weather warnings, There's blizzards, there's ice storms, this is the worst time of year to go. I took a chance, I went anyway, the weather was perfect, there was no traffic, and hardly anyone in the park. The famous Yosemite Falls, at 2,425 feet, one of the tallest on the planet, was dumping the snowpack of the high Sierras into the magnificent Merced River. The white man named this waterfall Bridal Veil and invented a stupid legend like if you walk under it You may soon be wed. The real story is if you walk under it, you'll soon be wet. The Indians who used to live here had a different name. They called it Poho Noh, which means puffing wind, a place where evil spirits dwell. And here is Half Dome, a rock climber's heaven. It's only killed thirty people since 1915, not bad. And this is El Capitan, where I get to make believe I'm Ansel Adams. And this marvel of rustic architecture opened in 1927 is the Awani Hotel, built by robber barons to entertain the world's elite like presidents and kings and movie stars and such. They'd sit around rooms like this with murals of Yosemite's wildlife on the walls and drink Whiskey, Cognac, Smoke Cigars, Gaffaw, Hangout next to the corner fireplace. It still costs a ton of money to stay there. If you can get in, it's usually sold out. But the most amazing thing about my visit to Yosemite in March of 2017 was this. Waterfalls where people had never seen waterfalls before. Some old timers told me that waterfalls in front of the lodge haven't been visible in a hundred years. It looked like water was coming directly out of the rocks. And with the droughts we're now seeing in the west, the global warming, these are visuals you may never see again. Who knows? The crows. Who cares? The bears. And even though there are about 500 black bears in the National Park, the only place I saw one was on the wall. The Park Service is doing a pretty good job of keeping them away from people. That's it for this edition of Maui Travels. If you have a trip you'd like to share, send it in. We'd love to see it.

stories.text: The County of Maui is dedicated to helping our residents return home, We're committed to building back stronger and more resilient, while working to maintain all that makes Lahaina so special. stories.headline: Prince Kūhiō Day closures and a look at his life

stories.text: Jonah Kūhiō Kalani-ana’ole was born in Koloa, Kauaʻi on March 26, 1871 to his parents, David Kahalepoili and his mother, Victoria Kūhiō Kinoikeke Kaulike. He had two brothers, David Kuananakoa and Edward Kealiʻi Ahunui. As young boys, Kūhiō and his brother, David ʻKoʻana Nakoa were Hana'i'd by his aunt and uncle, King Kalākawa and Queen Kapi'olani. And later, he actually served in the Department of Interior as the minister for his Hana'i father, King Kalākawa. After the overthrow in 1895, Robert Wilcox led a rebellion against the Republic of Hawaiʻi, and Kūhiō was a key player in this counterrevolution. Because Because of this act, he was charged for treason and spent one year in prison. And during that time he was visited every day by his sweetheart, Elizabeth Kahanu Kaʻauaʻi. And after he was released, they got married. And he won in 1902 a landslide victory election against Robert Wilcox to take the U.S. Congress seat. Kūhiō became a key player in the Hawaiian system of government that we know today. For instance, he has helped to establish the county He also pushed for the first bill of statehood for Hawaiʻi in 1919, and he advocated for Hawaiian Homes Commission Act for many years until it finally passed in Congress in 1921. Although Kūhiō was highly against the blood quantum restrictions imposed by the Hawaiian Commission Act, The Hawaiian Commission's office has granted over 10,000 families homestead lots so that they could return back to their ʻāina. The Hawaiian Homestead Act was passed in 1921. Kūhiō passed on January 7, 1922. stories.summary: Congresswoman Jill Tokuda told a large crowd at a town hall that everyone must fight back against the Trump administration's assault on immigrants, federal worker firings and education, and a testifier said the Democratic minority is giving no direction.
stories.text: There are so many issues that have come up with this new administration. One of them that is particularly bothersome is immigration problems in And I was wondering what do you have in the way of a plan to mitigate that? Well, first of all, let me just say that while there have been many, many concerns that I have with this administration that the community has, if there's been one silver lining, it's that people are coming out to town halls like this. They're voicing their displeasure, their concern, they're putting forward solutions. And so that community advocacy and engagement is a great thing to see. But immigration is one of those things that we cannot be passive about. If you think about all of us, for many of us, we're not too many generations away from when we were immigrants to this country, to this place that we now call home. I'm a Yonze, fourth generation. And so for me, making sure we protect the rights of those who have recently arrived, we know circumstances might differ, we know we don't have a perfect immigration system ourselves here in the United States. We must move with compassion and humanity. It's not something I have seen from this administration, literally ripping children out of schools. Where are our sensitive places? Another issue is the federal layoffs. And in particular, in our state parks, like Haleakalā, they let go a number of federal workers up there that were specifically trained to work with the endangered bird population, and now they're gone. And that's basically a death sentence to endangered birds. Yes, we'll even think about the fact that on certain years, depending on tourism, you can have over a million people going up to Haleakalā visiting. We need to keep people safe. We need to make sure that we are being true to our conservation efforts, like protecting endangered wildlife, endangered plant species. You can't do that if you don't have any staff. And if there's anything we know living on islands, you can let go even just a few people, and that might mean that Maui has zero physical presence. That's unacceptable, again. And When we think of all these indiscriminate firings and layoffs, even the courts are rejecting the idea right now. It is harmful to everyday life. Right now, they're scared as to where that next paycheck will come from. If they'll have a job, if they get called back, will they just be fired again? And so if you think about, Again, the humanity, the human impact behind these inhumane cuts. We have to remember they have faces, they have names. Look around you in Hawaiʻi. We're just one degree separation away from really being close to that hurt and harm. Given the paucity and the seeming invisibility of the democratic leadership right now, and I mean Chuck Schumer, I mean Akif Jeffries, I mean Kamala Harris, I mean the DNC, Has anyone shared any plan, blueprints, or way forward for your House, your Senate colleagues, Democrats in the field, governors, people that work at the local level, or us, all in this room, for things for us to do because we are hungry and starving for direction? stories.text: Pacific Biodiesel is the oldest biodiesel company in America. We had the first commercial biodiesel pump open to the public in the United States. Aloha, I'm Kelly King, founder of Pacific Biodiesel with my husband Bob King. We're here on our farm on Maui, 114 acres. Civic Biodiesel is a renewable fuel company. We make clean burning biodiesel for diesel engines out of used cooking oil. So we're taking a very caustic substance that used to go into the landfill and now we're turning it into a really nice clean burning locally made fuel. The sunflowers that we grow here are part of that whole sustainable model and we make culinary oils out of the sunflowers. That's being sold to the restaurants here. We then take the used cooking oil from the restaurants and make it into biodiesel. The restaurants are now part of the whole sustainability loop. All of the equipment on this farm runs on 100% biodiesel. I believe we're the only farm, maybe even in the state of Hawaiʻi, running on 100% renewable energy. It's really important to create biodiversity. We've been monocropping for hundreds of years in the state of Hawaiʻi, and it's really killed a lot of the soil. We've used zero pesticides on this farm. We are actually working towards no-till right now. We're doing some tilling because we're working on land that was farmed in sugarcane. But the goal is to get to no-till, to do things as healthy as possible. Cover cropping works. We're doing cow peas, but you can use sun ham, you can use chickpeas. And those are actual crops that if you weren't turning them in, put the nitrogen back into the soil, then you know it grows. If you ever wanted to pivot and go, now we're going to grow chickpeas, we can put that in and we know it grows and we know how it grows, the market may be there. Some of the other practices that we're doing are water conservation. So that's why we got the pivot and we were able to access a United States government program to give us a loan for the pivot. stories.text: Four artists have been selected as the State of Hawaiʻi's climate artists-in-residence. The innovative program seeks to engage local artists in the development of Hawaiʻi's climate action pathways, called CAP, through creating works across a range of artistic media. The artists will engage in the development of key topics from the CAP, including cultural knowledge, land stewardship, energy efficiency, transportation decarbonization, and community resilience. Artists will participate in subject matter meetings throughout the year and will have a chance to visit related projects on the ground. The finished artworks will be exhibited at the Capitol Modern, the Hawaiʻi State Art Museum in Honolulu, from October 1st through the 31st of this year.

stories.summary: The Senate passed SB 332 SD1 to require foreclosed homes to be sold separately, while the House companion bill HB 467 HD1 remains stalled in committee.
stories.text: The Hawaii Senate passed SB 332 SD 1, which prohibits bundling foreclosed homes at public sales, ensuring each home is sold separately. stories.headline: Rip current safety tips for beachgoers
stories.summary: A safety video explains that rip currents cause most beach rescues and advises staying calm, floating, swimming parallel to shore and signaling for help.
stories.text: We all love the beach in the summer, the sun, the sand, and the surf. But just because we're having fun doesn't mean we can forget about safety. Grit currents account for 80% of beach rescues and can be dangerous or deadly if you don't know what to do. It's simple stuff, but we can't take it for granted. Know before you go. Check local beach forecasts before you head to the beach and always swim near lifeguards. Look for any warning signs or flags. If you're unsure about conditions, Ask a lifeguard. And know how to swim before you venture in. If you do happen to be caught in a rip current, stay calm. It won't pull you under. It'll just pull you away from shore. If you try to fight the rip current and swim against it, you'll just... Get worn out. Instead, float. If you're a good swimmer, swim parallel to shore until you've cleared the pool of the rip current. Swim with the waves, allowing them to push you to shore. If you can, wave and yell to get the attention of lifeguards and people on shore to let them know you need help. Help! Be calm. You can stay safe and continue to have fun in the surf, sand and sun.

stories.headline: Hawaiʻi attorney general joins brief backing fired NLRB member
stories.summary: Attorney General Anne Lopez joined 20 attorneys general in an amicus brief in Wilcox v. Trump, urging the court to reinstate NLRB member Gwynne Wilcox.
stories.text: Hawaii Attorney General Anne Lopez joined 20 Attorneys General in an amicus brief for Wilcox v. Trump, challenging President Trump's removal of NLRB member Gwynne Wilcox. Her dismissal left the National Labor Relations Board without a quorum, effectively halting its operations. The coalition argues that a functioning NLRB is essential for enforcing U.S. labor laws and urges the court to reinstate Wilcox. The NLRB, established back in 1935, protects workers' rights to unionize, to bargain, and strike under the National Labor Relations Act.

stories.headline: Hirono and Blumenthal introduce bill to ban high-capacity magazines
stories.summary: Sens. Mazie Hirono and Richard Blumenthal introduced the Keep Americans Safe Act to reinstate a nationwide ban on magazines holding more than 10 rounds.
stories.text: U.S. Senators Maisie Hirono and Richard Blumenthal, both members of the Senate Judiciary Committee, introduced the Keep Americans Safe Act to reinstate a nationwide ban on the sale, transfer, possession, import or manufacture of high-capacity gun magazines that hold more than 10 rounds. A federal law prohibiting semi-automatic assault weapons and high-capacity magazines was in place from 1994 to 2004. While research showed this regulation reduced the likelihood of mass shooting fatalities by 70 percent, this federal law has not been renewed since 2004.

stories.text: Micah Labuanan and Jalea Miguel, close friends on and off the mats, kept their remarkable legacies in Maui Interscholastic League wrestling emphatically with the HHSAA State Championships February 22nd at the Neil Blais Del Arena. Labuanan Kamehameha Schools Maui Senior became the first EMAO boy to ever win four state wrestling titles, rolling to the 150-pound crown with two pins and two technical falls over the two-day state wrestling tournament. Miguel, a Baldwin High School senior, won her third state crown with four straight pins at 170 pounds. She became just the fourth MIL girl to win a third state title. Congratulations to you both.
